en: The *Bhikṣu-śrāvaka-dāna-sūtra*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmaruci of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. At that time...
There was a certain bhikṣu who went to the lecture hall where the other bhikṣus were and said to them:
"Venerable sirs!
Now I find the discourses and the Dharma unbearable; I am overcome by great sleepiness, I take no delight in practicing the Path, and I have doubts regarding the discourses and the Dharma."
Among those seated, there was a bhikṣu who immediately went to inform the Buddha:
"A bhikṣu named Śrutasoma has come to the lecture hall and said to the other bhikṣus:
'Now I find the sūtras and dharmas intolerable; I am overcome by great sleepiness, I take no pleasure in the practice of the Path, and I have doubts regarding the sūtras and dharmas.'"
The Buddha then replied: "This bhikṣu is deluded;

he does not guard the doors of his sense faculties, he does not eat moderately, he does not practice vigilance during the first and last watches of the night, and he does not contemplate wholesome dharmas. How, then, could he master the teachings of the sūtras, remain free from drowsiness, delight in the practice of the Path, and have no doubts regarding the teachings of the sūtras?"
"Even if one listens to the teachings, one will never attain this through such means.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:

"If one does not guard the doors of the sense faculties, does not eat moderately, does not practice vigilance during the first and last watches of the night, and does not contemplate wholesome dharmas—how could such a person transcend sleepiness, delight in the practice of the Path, and remain free from doubt regarding the teachings? One will never attain this through such means."

If a bhikṣu guards the doors of the sense faculties, eats moderately, remains alert and practices with diligence during the first and last watches of the night, contemplates wholesome dharmas, accords with the sūtras and the Dharma, abandons sleepiness, delights in the practice of the Path, and has no doubt regarding the sūtras and the Dharma—then from this, he may attain this.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"Go and call [the donor] to come and receive the gift.
The bhikṣu then rose, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, and went to call the donor to receive the gift.
Śroṇa immediately went to the Buddha's dwelling, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, and took his seat.
The Buddha then said: "Śroṇa! Speak whatever you desire."
Śraddhā said:
"My present body cannot grasp the sutras and dharmas; I am deeply overcome by sleep, take no pleasure in practicing the Path, and harbor doubts regarding the various sutras and dharmas.
The Buddha spoke to Śraddhā:
“I wish to ask you about a certain matter; please explain it according to what you know.
The Buddha said:

“Do you know that when one does not depart from lust for forms, does not depart from desire, does not depart from longing, does not depart from yearning, and does not depart from affection, then at the time of separation from those forms, there arise other transformations—sorrow, lamentation, pain, agitation, and despair—is this so? “It is so.”
The donor replied,
"Such and such a number [of people] came from there.
The Buddha said:
"Excellent! Excellent!
Worthy one, it is as you have said."
“Grant me leave to speak!
The Buddha said:

“If one does not depart from those [aggregates], and if one perceives feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—if a person is not separated from craving for consciousness, not separated from desire, not separated from longing, not separated from passion, and not separated from affection—then at the time of being separated from that consciousness, do other transformations arise: namely, sorrow, lamentation, pain, agitation, and despair? Is there not such a thing?”
Upon hearing the donor say,
"He has this," the Buddha said:
“Excellent! Excellent!
Worthy one, it is as you have said.”
"Listen to my teaching!
the Buddha said.

"If one does not depart from that [state], how could one know departure? When one is detached from form, detached from desire, detached from longing, detached from yearning, and detached from craving, and when that form is separated, no other transformation arises—neither sorrow, lamentation, pain, agitation, nor mental distress. Does such a state exist or not?"
Upon hearing the donor say,
"He has this," the Buddha said:
"Excellent! Excellent!
It is as the worthy one has said."
"Listen to my teaching!
The Buddha said:

"Just as one is detached from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—if one does not crave consciousness, and is without desire, without longing, without yearning, and without attachment—then at the time of being separated from that consciousness, no other transformation arises: namely, sorrow, lamentation, pain, agitation, or despair. Is it possible for such things to exist in one who is thus tranquil?"
Upon hearing the donor say,
"He has this," the Buddha said:
"Excellent! Excellent! It should be so."
“Listen to the gift!
The Buddha then granted permission for the gift, saying:
“I wish to preach the Dharma for you—a teaching that is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end.”
“If you will fully explain this path of practice from beginning to end— how it is entirely virtuous, wholesome, and excellent—
I shall listen and take it to heart.
Śīla replied, “Yes, I shall.”
The Buddha said:
"Once there were two people who set out together upon a road; one of them was familiar with the path, while the other was not."
One who does not know the path goes to ask one who knows the path, saying:
"I wish to go to a certain village, town, district, county, or kingdom; please tell me the way by which I should travel."
The one who knows the path said:
"Follow this road, proceeding straight to the right; you will encounter two paths. Abandon the left and take the right, proceeding straight to the right for a short while until you see a valley.
Above that valley there will again be two paths; abandon the left and take the right, proceeding straight to the right for a short while until you see a grove of trees."

Above the grove of trees there shall likewise be two paths; abandon the left path and take the right path, proceeding straight ahead for a short while until you gradually reach the village, town, district, or kingdom you desire to go to.
The Buddha said:
“Regarding the parable I have just related, you should know that all that has been spoken must likewise be contemplated with careful attention.
When I spoke of those who do not understand the path, this refers to the deviant paths of the world, as well as the teachings of those who hold to various forms of heterodoxy.”
"One who understands the path at its source" refers to the Tathāgata’s non-attachment to perfect enlightenment, as well as to those who have realized that perfect enlightenment.
"The paths said to be deviant" refers to the three evil thoughts of wicked people: first, sensual desire;
second, ill will; [and third, harmful intent].
Third is the thought of malice—this also refers to wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong resolve, wrong action, wrong effort, wrong concentration, and wrong liberation.
"Furthermore, what is called the 'right path' refers to the three wholesome reflections—first, the reflection on renunciation;
second, the reflection on non-confusion;
and third, the reflection on non-harming—and it also refers to right view, right mindfulness, right speech, right intention, right conduct, right effort, right resolve, and right concentration."
"What are called the two paths refers to what people doubt;
what are called the ravines and valleys refers to anger;
and what are called the thickets refer to the five pleasures."
First, the eye delights in forms, whereby craving for beautiful colors leads to attachment;
second, the ear delights in sounds;
third, the nose delights in fragrances.
Fourth, the tongue delights in flavors;
fifth, the body delights in what is fine and soft, and through desire one may become greedily attached to beautiful forms.
What is referred to as the assembly of villages, districts, counties, and kingdoms refers to the virtue of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The Buddha told them to accept the offerings, saying:
"These are matters of the Buddhas; I have spoken of them out of a heart of compassion. Those who wish to be delivered and liberated, I have already taken pity upon them."
Now, regarding those matters, one should practice with single-minded devotion in a secluded place beneath a tree in a state of tranquility;
or, in the mountains, marshes, or among burial mounds, one should subsist on fruits and gourds as food.
"Monks, do not be greedy for sensual desires; you will regret it later when dwelling in the world.
This is the practice of all Buddhas, and this is the teaching of all Buddhas.
Now that the Buddha has spoken thus, the worthy one listened with joy and reflected upon what the Buddha had said.
The Sūtra on the Ordination of Bhikṣus through Receiving Offerings.
